sentences.text: Nesodactylus possessed longer wings, more robust limbs, and longer legs than its relative Rhamphorhynchus, despite being of similar overall size.
Barnum Brown collected the remains of Nesodactylus in 1918 from rocks known for marine fossils but did not prepare them at that time.
Richard Lund revealed the pterosaur remains in 1966 by preparing seven black chalkstone blocks using acid to dissolve the surrounding rock.
Ned Colbert described and named the genus Nesodactylus in 1969.
James A. Jensen and John Ostrom mistakenly referred to Nesodactylus as Nesodon in 1977.

The holotype specimen — the specimen the species is based on — includes a partial skeleton with a skull fragment, vertebrae, a deeply keeled sternum, limbs, and ribs, though bones were not completely removed during preparation.
Nesodactylus is classified as a member of the rhamphorhynchid family.
Recent scientific reviews disagree on whether Nesodactylus belongs to the subfamily Rhamphorhynchinae or remains unclassified within that group.
Nesodactylus lived during the middle-late Oxfordian age of the Upper Jurassic in the Jagua Formation of western Cuba.
Nesodactylus lived between 161.5 and 143.1 million years ago, spanning the Oxfordian to Tithonian stages.
